summary: The note argues that technology is democratizing architectural heritage conservation, giving community members and amateur preservationists tools once reserved for high-budget projects. It covers DIY documentation (photogrammetry, drones), BIM software, material and structural analysis (pXRF, infrared thermography), augmented reality, crowdsourcing platforms, and green energy modeling. It concludes that these tools let individuals protect buildings and engage their communities.
one_line: Accessible technologies like photogrammetry, BIM, AR and crowdsourcing are letting amateur preservationists document, analyze and restore local historic architecture.
key_facts: The note is set in the latter part of 2023 and says that, more pointedly after September 1, 2023, the tools used in architectural heritage conservation have been significantly transformed.
Dr. Abigail Emerson, a leading architectural conservator, says: "What we're witnessing is the democratization of preservation tools."
Emerson says high-res scanning, 3D modelling software and even augmented reality are now in the hands of local societies and individual enthusiasts.
Modern smartphone cameras can be used for DIY photogrammetry by taking multiple photographs of a structure from various angles.
Free photogrammetry software named in the note includes Meshroom and COLMAP, used to create detailed 3D models.
Drones can give aerial views of tall or intricate buildings and help inspect parts of a building that are out of sight.
Building Information Modeling (BIM) integrates physical and functional characteristics into a digital representation; Autodesk's Revit and SketchUp (with BIM extensions) are named as tools.
Portable X-ray fluorescence (pXRF) analyzers let amateurs determine the elemental composition of building materials on-site, helping identify original materials.
Smartphone-attachable infrared thermography cameras detect thermal anomalies such as moisture ingress or insulation defects without damaging the structure.
Augmented reality apps let preservationists visualize restoration work before any physical changes and help educate the public about conservation.
Platforms like Historypin encourage community members to share old photographs, memories and historical insights about buildings.
Michael Patterson, founder of the local heritage app "PastView," says crowdsourcing historical data fosters "a sense of stewardship within the community."
Energy modeling software and life-cycle assessment tools help amateur preservationists plan energy-efficient retrofitting and green building practices so restoration stays eco-friendly.
